User: I need help with my 2023 tax return. I'm head of household in Chicago IL. My W-2 from TechStart Inc shows $64,800. I had $15,000 in 1099 income (marketing, 2 clients), $1,450 from Goldman Sachs Marcus, and $320 from TD Ameritrade. I have a home office (140 sq ft, exclusive use); rent is $2,400/month for 620 sq ft total. Student loan interest: $3,600 (Navient, 2017–2019). I donated $1,350 to St. Mary's Food Bank (have the receipt) have receipt, and had $1,350 in work expenses. What can I deduct, and should I itemize or take the standard deduction? What forms do I need?
Assistant: I can help — here’s a clear, practical breakdown of what you can likely deduct, whether you should itemize, which federal (and a note about state) forms you’ll need, and a few clarifying questions.

Quick summary / recommendation
- Most likely: take the Head‑of‑Household standard deduction ($20,800 for 2023). With the items you gave, your itemized deductions (charity $1,350 plus any state/local taxes/property taxes) will most likely be less than $20,800 unless you have large unreported SALT or other itemizable amounts.
- You must report your 1099 income and business expenses on Schedule C and pay self‑employment tax (Schedule SE). Because you have self‑employment income and a qualifying, exclusively used home office, you can take a home‑office deduction (actual method will be much larger than the simplified method in your facts).
- Student loan interest: up to $2,500 above‑the‑line deduction may be available (subject to income limits). I need to confirm the $3,600 you cited is interest paid in 2023 (see questions below).
- Work expenses: whether they’re deductible depends on whether they’re employee unreimbursed expenses (generally not deductible for 2018–2025) or ordinary business expenses of your 1099 work (deductible on Schedule C).

Details and calculations (approximate)
1) Income to report
- W-2 wages: $64,800
- 1099 (self‑employment) gross: $15,000 — report on Schedule C
- Interest income: $1,450 + $320 = $1,770 — taxable interest; because total interest > $1,500, you’ll likely need Schedule B

Total gross income ≈ $81,570 (before business expense deductions and adjustments).

2) Self‑employment (1099) treatment and business deductions
- Report gross 1099 income on Schedule C.
- Business expenses: you said $1,350 in work expenses — if these are expenses of your 1099 marketing work (supplies, advertising, software, mileage, phone portion, etc.) they are deductible on Schedule C.
- Home office (you stated exclusive use, 140 sq ft of 620 sq ft):
  - Percentage = 140 / 620 = ~22.58%.
  - Rent: $2,400/mo × 12 = $28,800/year. Allocable to business (rent × 22.58%) ≈ $6,504.
  - If you also allocate utilities, internet, renter’s insurance portion, that increases the deduction.
  - Simplified home‑office option would be 140 sq ft × $5 = $700 — clearly smaller than the actual allocation using the rent share above. For your facts the actual (share of rent) is likely better.
- Estimated Schedule C net profit (very approximate): 15,000 − (1,350 + 6,504) ≈ $7,146 net profit.
- Self‑employment tax (Schedule SE): SE tax applies to ~92.35% of net self‑employment earnings. Using the approx net above, SE tax will be due (and half of that SE tax is an above‑the‑line deduction on Form 1040).

3) Student loan interest
- The student loan interest deduction (Form 1040 adjustment) allows up to $2,500 of interest paid in the tax year, subject to income phaseouts. For single / HOH the 2023 MAGI phaseout begins around $75,000 and phases out to $90,000 (verify exact MAGI limits if you’re near this range).
- Clarify: is the $3,600 the amount of interest you actually paid in 2023? (You can only deduct the amount paid in 2023, and up to $2,500 maximum.)

4) Charitable donations
- $1,350 cash donation to a qualified charity is deductible, but only if you itemize (Schedule A). If you take the standard deduction, you cannot also deduct that charitable donation on Schedule A.

5) Employee unreimbursed “work expenses”
- If those $1,350 expenses are for your W‑2 job and were unreimbursed, they are not deductible for tax years 2018–2025 for most taxpayers (suspended by TCJA). If those expenses are for your self‑employment (1099) activity, they belong on Schedule C instead (deductible).

Should you itemize vs. take the standard deduction?
- The 2023 standard deduction for Head of Household is $20,800. With only $1,350 in charitable donations and no mortgage interest or large medical or property tax amounts provided, it is very likely the standard deduction will be larger than your itemized deductions.
- Items that could push you to itemize: meaningful property taxes, state income taxes up to the SALT cap ($10,000 total), mortgage interest, large medical expenses above 7.5% of AGI, or other large deductible amounts.
- Recommendation: unless you have additional itemizable amounts (SALT close to $10k, mortgage interest, large unreimbursed medical expenses), take the standard deduction.

Forms you’ll likely need (federal)
- Form 1040 (U.S. Individual Income Tax Return)
- Schedule 1 (additional income and adjustments) — Schedule C net profit flows into Schedule 1 and adjustments (student loan interest, half of SE tax, etc.) are reported here
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — report the $15k 1099 income and all business expenses (including home office share, supplies, etc.)
- Schedule SE (Self‑Employment Tax) — compute SE tax on net self‑employment earnings
- Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) — if you use the actual home‑office method to compute allocable expenses (some filers use this; with simplified method you don’t use 8829). Note: because you rent, you cannot claim depreciation on the home, but Form 8829 is commonly used to compute the home office deduction when using actual expenses.
- Schedule B (Interest and Ordinary Dividends) — required if interest or ordinary dividends > $1,500 (your interest total is $1,770)
- Schedule A (Itemized Deductions) — only if you decide to itemize (probably not needed)
- Illinois: IL‑1040 (Illinois individual income tax return) — you’ll also file the state return. Illinois has a flat rate and allows limited deductions (check withholding and credits).

Records to keep
- Receipts for charitable contribution(s) — you have a receipt for the $1,350 donation (good).
- Receipts/invoices for your 1099 work expenses and any files documenting home office use (floor plan, exclusive use statement) and copies of lease and rent paid.
- 1099‑NEC/1099‑MISC forms from clients, 1099‑INT for interest, W‑2 from employer, Form 1098‑E if you have one for student loan interest (or a 1098‑E or interest statement from Navient).

A short worked example (approx.)
- W‑2: $64,800
- 1099 gross: $15,000
- Interest: $1,770
- Business expenses incl. home office (actual share of rent + $1,350): ≈ $7,854
- Approx net SE income ≈ $7,146 → SE tax ≈ $1,010 (half ≈ $505 deductible)
- If eligible for full $2,500 student loan interest deduction, that reduces AGI further.
- After the standard deduction $20,800 (HOH), you’ll likely have a substantially lower taxable income than any itemized scenario with only $1,350 charity.

Questions I need from you to be precise
1. Did you actually pay $3,600 in student loan interest in 2023 (i.e., payments made during 2023), or is $3,600 the cumulative interest from 2017–2019? Only interest paid in 2023 is potentially deductible on the 2023 return.
2. Are the $1,350 in “work expenses” expenses related to your 1099 marketing business (i.e., self‑employment) or are they unreimbursed expenses for your W‑2 job? (If they’re for the 1099 business, they’re deductible on Schedule C; if for W‑2 employment, they’re generally not deductible.)
3. Do you have any other deductible items not listed (property tax paid in 2023, state income tax paid, mortgage interest, large medical expenses, or other donations)? If you have significant SALT or mortgage interest, itemizing might become beneficial.
4. Do you own the home or rent? (You said rent — that confirms you don’t have depreciation on the structure.)

Other notes and recommendations
- If you’d like, I can run a more precise estimated tax calculation if you confirm the answers to the questions above (particularly the student‑loan interest paid in 2023 and whether the $1,350 are 1099 business expenses).
- Because you have self‑employment income, consider whether you need to make/adjust estimated tax payments for 2024 to avoid underpayment penalties.
- I’m not a CPA — for complex situations or to finalize returns, consider confirming these results with a tax professional or using tax software.

If you want, I can:
- Estimate your federal tax owed/refund with the numbers you gave (I’ll need the clarifications above).
- Draft an email to your CPA with the figures and documents you have (I can create and send/draft it for you). Which would you prefer?
